subject: Climate & Environment
title: How Forests Cool the Planet
description: A micro-lesson that makes How Forests Cool the Planet usable.

hook.text: Walk from a parking lot into a forest. The temperature drops several degrees instantly.

buildup.text: Trees shade the ground, reflect sunlight, and release water vapor that cools the air.

discovery.text: Large forests can lower regional temperatures by 1-3°C compared to cleared land.

twist.text: Deforested areas absorb more heat from the Sun, creating local warming on top of global warming.

climax.text: Tropical forests cool the planet both by storing carbon and by physically lowering temperatures.

punchline.text: Forests are Earth's air conditioning. We keep switching them off.

quiz.question: How do forests physically cool the surrounding area?

details.summary: Forests cool the planet through three mechanisms: absorbing CO2, releasing water vapor through transpiration that forms clouds, and having lower albedo effects that shade the surface. Tropical forests provide the strongest cooling effect of any land ecosystem.
details.whyItMatters: Deforestation removes a natural cooling system alongside its carbon storage. Forest cooling effects compound the climate damage of clearing beyond what CO2 release alone shows.
takeaways: Tropical forests cool locally by 2 to 8 degrees through evapotranspiration
Forest transpiration creates clouds that reflect sunlight
Deforestation removes both carbon storage and cooling services

faq.question: How much do forests cool their surroundings?
faq.answer: Tropical forests can be 2 to 8 degrees cooler than nearby cleared land due to evapotranspiration. This cooling extends beyond the forest through moisture transport and cloud formation, moderating temperatures across wide regions.

faq.question: Do all forests cool the planet equally?
faq.answer: Tropical forests provide the most cooling because they transpire year-round and reflect sunlight effectively. Boreal forests absorb significant sunlight due to dark needles, which partially offsets their carbon benefits with a local warming effect on snow-covered land.
